title: Primary, secondary and tertiary sources; credibility
blurb: Sort any source into primary, secondary or tertiary, and judge how far to trust it using currency, relevance, authority, accuracy and purpose.
question: For a report on the 1918 flu, a student has a nurse's diary from 1918, a 2015 biography of a doctor who treated flu patients, and an encyclopedia entry on pandemics. A TEAS item asks which is the primary source, and many students pick the biography. Why is that wrong?

teach.body: Formally, a primary source is firsthand: created at the time of an event or by a participant, or reporting original data. A secondary source analyzes, interprets or summarizes primary sources. A tertiary source compiles or indexes secondary sources for quick reference. In plain English: primary is 'I was there' or 'here is my original data'; secondary is 'here is what it means'; tertiary is 'here is a quick overview.'

teach.caption: Each level is built on the one beneath it.

teach.h: Classifying a source in three questions
items: Was the creator there, or does it report its own original data? Then it is primary.
Does it analyze, interpret or summarize primary sources written by others? Then it is secondary.
Does it compile secondary information into a reference work for quick lookup? Then it is tertiary.

teach.caption: Both articles may appear in the same journal. What matters is whether it reports its own study.

teach.text: Source-type traps: a biography or textbook called primary (both are secondary), an encyclopedia called secondary (it is tertiary), and a published research article reporting its own study called secondary (it is primary). An autobiography or memoir, written by the person who lived it, is primary.

teach.body: Any source can be judged on five points. Currency: when was it published or updated? Health information should be recent. Relevance: does it fit your need? Authority: who wrote it, with what expertise and for which publisher? Accuracy: are there evidence, citations, peer review and no obvious errors? Purpose: is it written to inform, or to sell or persuade, and who sponsors it?

teach.caption: Peer-reviewed journals and government health agencies are more reliable than blogs, forums, social media posts, ads and anonymous sites.

teach.body: Destiny Brooks, applying to an ADN program, sorts sources for a paper on the 1918 flu. The nurse's 1918 diary was written by someone who was there: primary. The 2015 biography interprets letters and records written by others: secondary, even though it is about a real person from that time. The encyclopedia entry compiles a brief overview: tertiary. For credibility she checks each author's expertise and publisher and whether the facts are cited.

items: Primary = firsthand or original data; secondary = interprets; tertiary = compiles.
Biographies, textbooks and review articles are secondary.
A research article reporting its own study is primary.
Encyclopedias, dictionaries and almanacs are tertiary.
CRAAP: currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, purpose; .org is not automatically unbiased.

summary: You can now classify a source as primary, secondary or tertiary, including the tricky cases such as biographies, research articles and review articles. You can also judge a source's credibility by its currency, relevance, authority, accuracy and purpose.

A.q: A student is writing a report about a 1994 nurses' strike at a city hospital. Which of the following is a primary source?
options: A letter written by a striking nurse to her sister in 1994
A 2012 history of labor unions that has a chapter on the strike
An encyclopedia entry summarizing major US hospital strikes
A 2020 documentary that explains the causes of the strike
A.why: A letter written during the strike by a nurse who took part is a firsthand account created at the time: a primary source.

whyNot.1: A later history interprets the event from other sources, so it is secondary.
whyNot.2: An encyclopedia compiles summaries for reference, so it is tertiary.
whyNot.3: A documentary made decades later interprets the event, so it is secondary.

A.q: A biography of Clara Barton, founder of the American Red Cross, was published in 2010 by a historian who studied Barton's letters and diaries. What type of source is the biography?
options: Primary, because it is about a real historical person
Tertiary, because it gathers facts about Barton's life
Secondary, because it interprets Barton's own writings
Primary, because it quotes Barton's letters and diaries
A.why: The historian analyzes and interprets Barton's letters and diaries, which are the primary sources. A biography written by someone else is secondary.

whyNot.0: Being about a real person does not make a work firsthand; the author was not there.
whyNot.1: Tertiary sources compile brief reference overviews; a full biography interprets sources.
whyNot.3: Quoting primary sources does not turn an interpretation into a primary source.

A.q: Which of the following is a tertiary source?
options: A medical journal article reporting a new vaccine trial
A textbook chapter explaining how vaccines are tested
A diary kept by a volunteer during a vaccine trial
An online encyclopedia entry on the history of vaccines
A.why: An encyclopedia compiles information from secondary sources into a brief reference overview, which makes it tertiary.

whyNot.0: An article reporting its own trial presents original data, so it is primary.
whyNot.1: A textbook explains and interprets research, so it is secondary.
whyNot.2: A participant's diary is a firsthand account, so it is primary.

B.q: A peer-reviewed journal article describes a study its authors ran on 400 patients, including their methods, data and results. How should the article be classified?
options: Secondary, because it was published in a journal
Primary, because it reports the authors' own study
Secondary, because it was reviewed by other experts
Tertiary, because it appears in a medical database
B.why: An article that reports the authors' own original study and data is a primary source, whatever journal or database it appears in.

whyNot.0: Being published in a journal does not make a source secondary; a review article would be.
whyNot.2: Peer review affects credibility, not whether a source is primary or secondary.
whyNot.3: Being listed in a database does not change the article itself into a tertiary source.

B.q: A student finds a well-designed website from a university medical center explaining the recommended vaccine schedule for children. The page was last updated in 2009. Which credibility factor should concern the student most?
options: Authority
Purpose
Relevance
Currency
B.why: Vaccine schedules are updated over time, so a page last updated in 2009 may be out of date. Currency is the main concern.

whyNot.0: A university medical center is a qualified authority.
whyNot.1: An educational page from a medical center is written to inform, not to sell.
whyNot.2: The page covers exactly the student's topic, so it is relevant.

B.q: A website ending in .org argues that a certain herbal supplement prevents colds. The site is run by a trade group of supplement makers and cites no studies. Which statement about the site is most accurate?
options: It is reliable because .org sites are run by nonprofits.
It is primary because the group makes the supplements.
Its purpose and lack of citations make it less credible.
It is current, so its claims can be accepted as accurate.
B.why: The site is run by people who profit from the supplement (purpose) and cites no evidence (accuracy). A .org address does not guarantee neutrality.

whyNot.0: .org sites vary; a .org address is not proof of reliability.
whyNot.1: Making a product does not turn an advocacy page into a firsthand source of evidence.
whyNot.3: Being current does not make unsupported claims accurate.

C.q: Which pair correctly classifies both sources?
options: Review article on sleep studies: primary; almanac: tertiary
Review article on sleep studies: secondary; almanac: tertiary
Review article on sleep studies: secondary; almanac: secondary
Review article on sleep studies: tertiary; almanac: primary
C.why: A review article summarizes and evaluates many studies, so it is secondary. An almanac compiles facts for quick reference, so it is tertiary.

whyNot.0: A review article does not report its own study, so it is not primary.
whyNot.2: An almanac compiles reference facts, so it is tertiary, not secondary.
whyNot.3: A review article interprets studies (secondary), and an almanac is not firsthand.

C.q: A documentary about World War II nurses includes clips from interviews recorded with nurses in 1946, along with a narrator's commentary added in 2019. For a research paper, which part counts as a primary source?
options: The documentary film taken as a whole work
The narrator's commentary recorded in 2019
The 1946 interview recordings with nurses
The 2019 on-screen summaries of the interviews
C.why: The 1946 interviews are firsthand accounts from participants, recorded close to the time, so they are primary sources, even when shown inside a secondary work.

whyNot.0: A documentary as a whole interprets events, so it is secondary.
whyNot.1: Commentary added decades later interprets the events, making it secondary.
whyNot.3: Summaries written in 2019 interpret the interviews after the fact, so they are secondary.

C.q: A student researching whether a common pain reliever is safe during pregnancy finds four sources. Which is likely the most credible?
options: A current guidance page from a federal government health agency
An advertisement from a company that makes the pain reliever
A popular parenting forum where many mothers share their stories
A 2008 magazine article by a journalist who interviewed a doctor
C.why: A current page from a government health agency is authoritative, up to date and written to inform rather than to sell.

whyNot.1: An ad from the maker has a financial interest in the product.
whyNot.2: Forum posts are personal stories, not expert evidence, however many there are.
whyNot.3: The article is outdated for a health question, and it is a secondhand account of one doctor's view.

reteach.title: Think of a concert
reteach.question: You were at a concert last night. Your friend reads your texts and writes a review. A music website later lists the tour in its year-end roundup. Which one is primary?

blocks.body: Your texts and phone videos from the front row are primary: you were there. Your friend's review interprets your texts and other reports, so it is secondary. The website's year-end list of tours compiles many reviews into a quick reference, so it is tertiary. And if the 'review' turns out to be written by the band's own manager, its purpose makes it less credible, however polished it looks.

blocks.text: A review written years later about a real concert is still secondary. Being about a real event does not make a source primary; being there (or producing the original data) does.

explain.body: Primary sources are firsthand: diaries, letters, speeches, photographs, interviews, autobiographies, eyewitness accounts, laws, raw data, patient records, videos of events and original research articles reporting their own study.

test.q: Which of these is a primary source on a city's 1985 flood?
options: A photograph of the flooded main street taken that day
A 2015 textbook chapter on floods in American cities
An encyclopedia article listing major US floods
A 2021 magazine essay on the city's flood history
test.why: A photograph taken on the day captures the event directly, so it is primary.

whyNot.1: A later textbook interprets events, so it is secondary.
whyNot.2: An encyclopedia compiles reference information, so it is tertiary.
whyNot.3: An essay decades later interprets the history, so it is secondary.

explain.body: Secondary sources analyze, interpret or summarize primary sources: textbooks, biographies, review articles, literature reviews, documentaries, news analysis and commentaries.

test.q: A literature review in a nursing journal summarizes 35 published studies on hand hygiene. What type of source is it?
options: Primary, because it appears in a nursing journal
Tertiary, because it gathers many studies together
Primary, because it includes data from 35 studies
Secondary, because it summarizes others' research
test.why: A literature review summarizes and evaluates other researchers' studies rather than reporting its own, so it is secondary.

whyNot.0: Appearing in a journal does not make an article primary; reporting its own study does.
whyNot.1: A literature review analyzes studies in depth; tertiary sources are brief reference works.
whyNot.2: Data drawn from others' studies is secondhand, not original.

explain.body: Tertiary sources compile or index information from secondary sources for quick reference: encyclopedias, dictionaries, almanacs, handbooks, indexes and fact books.

test.q: A student looks up 'hypertension' in a medical dictionary to check its definition. What type of source is the dictionary?
options: Primary
Tertiary
Secondary
Anecdotal
test.why: A dictionary compiles definitions for quick reference, which makes it a tertiary source.

whyNot.0: A dictionary does not report firsthand experience or original data.
whyNot.2: Secondary sources interpret primary sources in depth; a dictionary compiles brief entries.
whyNot.3: 'Anecdotal' describes a personal story, not a reference work.

explain.body: Check currency (date), relevance (fit), authority (author, publisher), accuracy (evidence, citations, peer review) and purpose (inform or sell; sponsor). A .org address does not guarantee neutrality.

test.q: A blog post about a new diabetes drug is written by an anonymous author, cites no sources and links to a site selling the drug. Which credibility factors are the main problems?
options: Currency and relevance
Relevance and accuracy
Authority and purpose
Currency and authority
test.why: An anonymous author gives no basis for trust (authority), and links to a seller suggest the goal is to sell (purpose). The missing citations add an accuracy problem.

whyNot.0: Nothing about the post's date is mentioned, and it is on topic.
whyNot.1: The post is on the topic, so relevance is not the problem.
whyNot.3: The date is not mentioned, so currency is not the clear issue.
